In order to create a right influence, one must believe in one’s similes oneself as if in realities; and that can only be done when one possesses the mystical tendency, and when the similes themselves are born of occult science. The real occultist does not need to worry about the above-mentioned simile of the soul going forth from the body, because for him it is a truth. To him the butterfly evolving from the chrysalis represents the same experience on a lower stage of nature’s existence as the going forth of the soul from the body at a higher stage development. He believes in it with all his might, and this belief flows forth as if in invisible streams from the speaker to the listener, and inspires conviction. Direct life-streams then flow forth from teacher to pupil. But for this end it is necessary for the teacher to draw from the full source of occult science; it is necessary that his word and all that goes forth from him, should be clothed with feeling, warmth and glowing emotion from the true occult view of life. For this reveals a magnificent perspective of the whole subject of education. Once the latter allows itself to be enriched from the life source of occult science, it will itself become permeated with a profound vitality. It will give up groping in the dark, so common in this particular domain of thought. All educational methods, all educational sciences, that do not continually receive a supply of fresh sap from such roots, are dried up and dead. For all world-secrets occult science has fitting similes, similes not rising from the mind of man but drawn from the essence of things, having been laid down as a basis by the forces of the world at their creation. Occult science must therefore be the basis for any system of education.

A power of the soul to which particular attention ought to be given at this period of development is that of memory. For the cultivation of the memory is connected with the transformation of the etheric body. This has its effect in the fact that precisely during the time between the coming of the second teeth and that of puberty it becomes free, so that this is also the period in which the further development of the memory should be looked after from outside. The memory will be permanently of less value to the person in question than it might have been, if at this period what is necessary to it is neglected. That which has thus been neglected cannot afterwards be retrieved.

An intellectual and materialistic way of thinking is liable to bring about many mistakes in this direction. A system of education arising from this way of thinking is easily prejudiced against that which is acquired merely by the memory. It will not tire at times of directing itself with the greatest ardor against the mere training of the memory, and rather makes use of the most ingenious methods that the young person may not mechanically absorb what he does not really understand. An opinion merely intellectual and materialistic is so easily persuaded that there is no means of penetrating into things except by abstract ideas; it is only with difficulty that thinkers of this kind come to the conclusion that the other subjective powers are at least just as necessary to the comprehension of things, as the intellect itself. It is not merely a figure of speech to say that one can understand just as well with the feelings, the emotions, the mind, as with the intellect. Ideas are only one of the means by which to understand the things of this world, and only to materialists do they appear the only means. There are, of course, many people who do not imagine that they are materialists, but who nevertheless consider an intellectual conception to be the only means of comprehension. Such men profess perhaps to hold an idealistic, perhaps even a spiritual conception of the world and life. But the attitude of their souls toward both is materialistic. For the intellect is, as a matter of fact, the soul’s instrument for the comprehension of material things.

And here, concerning the deeper foundations of the understanding, let us quote from that excellent educational book, by Jean Paul already mentioned—a work containing generally golden ideas concerning education and deserving of much more consideration than at present it receives. It is of much more value to the guardian than many of the writings on these lines that enjoy the highest repute. The passage under consideration runs thus:

“Do not be afraid of unintelligibility, even if it be of whole sentences; your look and the manner of your expression, added to the eager desire to understand, elucidates the one half, and with this, and in due time, the other half also. For with children, as with the Chinese and with men of the world, the manner of pronunciation is half the language. Bear in mind, that they understand their language as well as we understand Greek or any other foreign tongue before learning to speak it. Trust to the deciphering of time and to association. A child of five years of age understands indeed the words “yet,” “truly,” “on the contrary,” “of course”; but for a definition of them one must go not to the child, but to the father! The little word “but” reveals a small philosopher. If the eight-year-old child with his growing power of speech is understood by a child of three, why should you then confine your language to his babbling? Always speak several years in advance (for in books genius speaks to us centuries in advance); with the child of a year, speak as if it were two, with the child of two as if it were six, for the difference of growth may diminish in inverse proportion to the years. Generally speaking, all learning is apt to be too much ascribed to the credit of the teacher—therefore the teacher ought to bear in mind that the child possesses half his world, namely, the spiritual (such as his moral and metaphysical ideas), already complete and taught within himself, and that therefore a language composed only of concrete images can never impart spiritual ideas, but can only light them up. The joy and assurance used in speaking to children ought to be given as if the assurance and joy came from themselves. We can learn speech from them, just as we teach them by means of speech; by means of bold and yet correct word-painting, such as for instance I have heard spoken by children of three and four years of age: ‘leg-fish’ for otter; ‘pig-iron’ for the fork used in eating bacon; ‘the air-mouse’ (unquestionably superior to our word ‘bat’) and so on.”

It is true that this passage refers to the understanding (before the intellectual comprehension) as exercised in another sphere than that of which we are now speaking, but for this also, the words of Jean Paul have an important meaning. Just as the child receives into his soul’s organism the construction of speech, without making use of the laws of grammatical structure with intellectual comprehension, so too, for the cultivation of his memory, the youth ought to learn things of which he will not until later acquire an actual understanding. That which has been acquired in this period of life, at first in a purely mechanical way, is best put into ideas, afterwards, just as one learns more easily the rules of a language when one can already speak it. All the talk of work learned by rote and not understood is nothing more than a materialistic prejudice. For instance, the youth needs only to acquire by a few examples the most necessary rules of multiplication, for which the fingers are far better suited than an abacus, and then to learn fully, by rote, the multiplication table. If one so proceeds, one takes into account the nature of the growing child. But a mistake may be made with regard to this, if, during the time that the memory is forming itself, too much is demanded of the intellect. The intellect being a power of the soul, and only born at the time of puberty, ought not to receive an outward influence before this period. Until the time of puberty, the youth should assimilate into the memory treasures over which mankind has meditated; later on it is time to permeate with ideas that which has been impressed upon his memory. A man ought therefore not to retain merely what he has understood, but he ought now to understand the things that he knows; that is to say, the things of which he has already taken possession by means of the memory, just as the child does, when learning to speak. This applies to a wider sphere. At first, assimilation of historical events by mere rote, then comprehension of the same by means of ideas. At first, a good impression upon the memory of geographical data, then an understanding of the relationship of each thing with the rest, etc. In certain respects all comprehension through ideas should be done by means of the stored treasures of the memory. The more the youth already knows through the memory before he comes to comprehension, the better it is. It is hardly necessary to explain that all this applies only to the period, of which we are speaking, and not to any later period. If one learns a subject in later life, either by going over it again, or in any other way, the opposite process to that here described might be correct and desirable, although even then a great deal depends upon the particular spiritual nature of the student. But at the time of life of which we have already spoken the spirit must not be parched by being overcrowded with intellectual ideas.

It is also true that teaching by mere sense-objects, if carried too far, is the result of a materialistic view of life. At this age every idea must be spiritualised. One ought not, for instance, to be satisfied with merely producing a sense-impression of a plant, a grain of seed, or a blossom. Everything should seem as an allegory of the spiritual. A grain of seed is, in truth, not merely what it appears to the eye. Invisibly the whole new plant inhabits it, and that such a thing is more than what the sense perceives, must be absolutely realised with the perception, the imagination, and the feelings. The mysterious presence of latent existence must really be felt. Nor can it be objected that such a proceeding would weaken the perception of pure sense; on the contrary, by a persistent adherence to sense perceptions alone, Truth itself would be the loser. For the complete reality of a thing exists in Spirit and in Matter, and accurate observations can be no less carefully carried out if one brings to the study not only the physical senses, but also the spiritual faculties. If people could only perceive, as the Occultist is able to, how both body and soul are spoiled by mere object-teaching, they would not then lay so much stress upon it. Of what value is it from the highest point of view, if young people are shown all kinds of physical experiments in the mineral, vegetable and animal worlds, if with such a study one does not suggest the application of the sense allegory to the feeling of spiritual mystery? Certainly a materialistic mind will not be able to make anything of what has here been said, and of that the Occultist is only too conscious. Yet it is also clear to him that a really practical method of education can never proceed from the materialistic mind. So practical does such a mind imagine itself, and yet so unpractical is it in reality, when it is a matter of considering life vitally. Opposed to the true reality, materialistic opinions seem only fantastic, while to the materialist, the interpretations of occult science must, of necessity, appear equally fantastic. Doubtless, too, there will remain many obstacles which must be overcome before the fundamental teachings of occult science, arising from life itself, will permeate the art of education. But that is to be expected, for at present these truths are strange to many; nevertheless, if they be really the truth, they will incorporate themselves into all culture.

Only through the sure conviction that they are the only educational means by which to work upon young people, can the teacher always find the right way to deal correctly with each individual case. Thus, he must know how the individual powers of the soul —such as thinking, feeling and willing—ought to be treated, and how their development may react upon the etheric body; while this itself, between the period when the second teeth appear and that of puberty, can be perfectly moulded by outside influences.

The foundations for the development of a healthy and powerful will can be laid by the right management, during the first seven years, of those fundamental principles of education which have already been considered. For such a will must have for its support the fully developed form of the physical body. From the period of the second teething it begins to be a matter of making the etheric body, which is now developing, supply those powers to the physical body by which it can solidify its form and make itself firm. That which makes the most vivid impression upon the etheric body also reacts most forcibly upon the strengthening of the physical. And the strongest impulses are evoked in the etheric body through those perceptions and ideas by which a person feels and experiences his own relation to the everlasting Universe, that is to say, through religious experiences. The will, and along with it, the character, of a person will never develop healthily if he cannot experience at this epoch of life, profound religious impulses. The result of the uniform organisation of the will is that the person feels himself to be an organic fragment of the whole world. If the person does not feel himself to be indissolubly connected with a Supreme Spirit, then must the will and character remain unstable, discordant and unhealthy.

The emotional nature is developed in the right direction by means of the allegories and sense-pictures already described, and especially by all which, whether from history or from other sources, presents to us the figures of persons with character. An absorption in the mysteries and beauties of Nature is also of importance in the upbuilding of the emotional world. And here it is particularly well to consider the culture of the sense of beauty, and the awakening of the feeling for what is artistic. Music should supply that rhythm to the etheric body which then enables it to perceive in everything the rhythm otherwise concealed. A young person will be deprived of much in all his after life, who does not receive at this period the benefit of cultivating the musical sense. To him in whom this sense is altogether lacking, a certain aspect of the Universe must remain hidden. Nor should, however, the other arts be, by any means neglected. The awakening of the sense for architectural form, as also for plastic shape, for line, design and harmony of color—not one of these ought to be omitted in the plan of education. So simply, perhaps, might all this be done, under special circumstances, that the objection that circumstances allow of no development at all in this direction can never be valid. One can do much with the simplest means, if the right sense in this direction prevails in the teacher himself. The joy of life, the love for existence, the strength to work—all these arise for the whole being, out of the cultivation of the sense of beauty and art. And the relations of man to man—how ennobled and how beautiful will they become through this sense! The moral sense, which will, at this period, be developed by pictures of life and by standard authorities, will also gain a certain stability if, through the sense of beauty, the good is recognized as beautiful and the bad as ugly.

Thought in its own shape, as an inner life of distilled ideas, must, at the period in question, be kept in the background. It must develop spontaneously, as it were, uninfluenced from without, while the soul is nourished by means of similes and pictures representing life and the mysteries of nature. Thus, in the midst of the other experiences of the soul between the seventh year and the time of puberty, thought must grow and the faculty for judgment be matured, so that after a successful puberty the person becomes capable of forming his own opinions concerning the matters of life and knowledge, with complete independence. Indeed, the less one works directly upon the critical faculty, and the more one works indirectly through the development of the other spiritual powers, the better will it be for the whole after-life of the person concerned.

Occult science lays down the principles, not only for the spiritual side of education, but also for the purely physical. Thus, to give a characteristic example, let us consider gymnastics and children’s games. Just as love and joy must permeate the environment during the first years of childhood, so too the growing etheric body must be taught really to experience from bodily exercise a feeling of its own expansion, of its ever increasing strength. For instance gymnastic exercises ought to be so carried out that with every movement, with every step, the feeling rises in the inner self of the boy or girl: “I feel increasing power within me.” And this feeling should manifest itself within as a healthy delight, as a sensation of pleasure. For the devising of gymnastic exercises, in this sense, it is of course necessary to possess more than a merely intellectual knowledge of the human body, anatomically and physiologically. It is necessary to possess a close intuitive and sympathetic knowledge of the relation of joy and comfort to the postures and movements of the human body. The formulator of such exercises ought himself to experience how one movement or posture of the limbs will produce a pleasant and comfortable sensation, but another a loss of strength, and so forth. A belief that gymnastics and bodily exercises can be cultivated in this direction is one that can only be supplied to the educator by occult science, or, above all, by a mind sympathetic to such thought. One does not even require the power of vision in the spiritual worlds, but only the inclination to apply to life what has been given out by occultism. If, especially in such practical departments as this of education, occult knowledge were applied, then all the useless talk of how this knowledge has yet to be proved would straightway cease. For to him who should rightly apply it, this knowledge would itself be a proof through the whole of life by making him healthy and strong. By such means he would perceive, through and through, that it is true in actual practice, and this he would find a better proof than any manner of “logical” and so-called “scientific” reasons. One can best know spiritual truths by their fruits, and not through a pretended proof, however scientific, for such could hardly be anything more than a logical skirmishing.

At puberty the astral body is first born. With the free outward development which follows, all that which is unfolded by the world of externalised perceptions, by one’s judgment and the unfettered understanding, will first rush inward upon the soul. It has already been mentioned that these faculties of the soul, hitherto uninfluenced from within, ought to be developed by the right management of educational means, just as unconsciously as the eyes and ears evolve themselves in the womb. But with puberty the time has arrived when the person is ready to form his own judgment concerning the things which he has hitherto learned. No greater injury can be inflicted on any one than by too soon awakening within him his own judgment. One should only judge when one has already stored up the necessary qualifications for judging and comparing. If, before this, one creates one’s own independent opinions, then these will have no sure foundations. All one-sidedness in life, all dreary “confessions of faith” which are based upon a few mere scraps of knowledge, and the desire to judge from these human conceptions that have been approved through long ages of time, rest upon just such mistakes in education. Before qualified to think, one must place before oneself, as a warning, what others have thought. There is no sound thinking which has not been preceded by a sound perception of the truth supported by obvious authority. If one wishes to follow out these principles of education, one must not allow people, at too early an age, to fancy themselves able to judge, for in avoiding this, one will leave them the possibility of allowing life to work upon them from every side, and without prejudice. For by one such judgment, which is not founded on the precious basis of spiritual treasures, he who makes it will have placed a stumbling-block in the path of his life. For if one has pronounced a judgment on any subject, one will always be influenced by having done so; one will no longer regard an experience as one might have regarded it, if one had not erected an opinion which is henceforth intertwined with the subject in question. In young people the disposition to learn first and then to judge, should be present. That which the intellect has to say of a certain subject ought only to be said when all the other powers of soul have spoken; before that the intellect ought only to play the part of mediator. It should only serve to lay hold of what is seen and felt, to apprehend it as it there exists, without allowing the unripe judgment to take possession of the matter. Therefore the youth ought to be shielded from all the theories concerning a thing, before the above-mentioned age, and it should be especially emphasized that he should face the experiences of life in order to admit them into his soul. A growing individual can certainly be made acquainted with what people have thought concerning this or that, but one should avoid letting him form opinions which arise from a premature judgment. He should receive opinions with the feelings, without deciding at once for one view or the other, not attaching himself to a party, but thinking, as he listens: “One has said this, and the other that.” Before all things a large measure of tact is necessary in the cultivation of this sense by teachers and guardians, but occult knowledge is exactly calculated to supply such tact.

It has only been possible to develop here a few aspects of education in the light of Occultism, but it has only been intended to give a hint as to what problems of civilisation this philosophy will have to solve. Whether it can do so depends on whether the inclination for such a way of thinking henceforth broadens out in ever widening circles. In order that this may take place, two things are necessary: first, that people should abandon their prejudice against Occultism. He who will truly associate himself with it, will soon see that it is not the fantastical trash which so many today imagine it to be. This is not intended as a reproach to such people, for everything which our time offers as a means of education must, at first, engender the view that occultists are fantastics and dreamers. On the surface any other view is hardly possible, for there appears to be the most complete diversity between what is known as Occult Science or Theosophy, and all that the culture of the present day suggests as the principles for a healthy view of life. Only a deeper consideration reveals to us how entirely in opposition the views of the present must remain without these principles of occult science—how, indeed, they themselves call out these very principles and in the long run cannot remain without them. The second thing that is necessary is connected with the sound development of Theosophy itself. Life will only welcome Theosophy, if in theosophical circles the knowledge is made to permeate everywhere that it is important to make these teachings bear fruit in the widest manner for all conditions of life, and not merely to theorize about them. Otherwise people will continue to look upon Theosophy as a kind of religious sectarianism, only fit for some fanatical enthusiasts. But if it performs positive useful spiritual work, then the theosophical movement cannot, in the long run, be refused an intelligent hearing.

The difference between the vegetable and the creature gifted with the power of sensation is completely lost sight of, because the essential characteristic of sensibility is not clearly defined. When a being (or an object) responds to an exterior impression by showing any effect whatever, it is inaccurate to conclude that this impression has been felt. To bear out this conclusion the impression must be experienced inwardly, that is to say, the outside stimulus must produce a kind of interior reflection. The great progress of natural science, which a true Theosophist must sincerely admire, has thrown our abstract vocabulary into confusion. Some of our biologists are ignorant of the characteristics of sensibility, and thus accredit it to beings who are devoid of it. Sensibility such as is comprehended by those biologists, can, it is true, be attributed to organisms deprived of it. But what is understood by Theosophy as sensibility is a totally different quality.

[3] A distinction must be made between the conscious inner life of the astral body and the perception of this life by outward clairvoyant observation. Here this latter perception by a trained clairvoyant is intended.

[4] The reader need not object to the technical term “Body of the ego,” because there is nothing of gross physical matter meant by it, but occult science being forced to employ the vocabulary of ordinary language, the words applied to Theosophy ought from the outset to be taken in a spiritual sense.

[5] The terms “Spirit-Self”, “Life-Spirit” and “Spirit-Man” need not mystify the reader; they stand for those transmutations of our grosser bodies which are the results of conscious effort and pure aspirations; they form, in other words, the Higher Trinity, called in Eastern terminology: Manas, Buddhi and Atma, respectively. (Trans.)

[6] Were these affirmations to be wrongly interpreted, the objection might be raised that a child before cutting his second teeth is not deprived of memory, and that before reaching the age of puberty, he possesses the inherent faculties of the astral body. It must not be forgotten that the etheric and astral bodies are in existence from the moment of physical birth, although surrounded by the protecting shell described. It is precisely this envelope, protecting the etheric body, which permits of a remarkably good memory before the cutting of the second teeth. The existence of physical eyes in the embryonic being, concealed in the womb of the mother, is analogous. And in the same way that the physical eyes sheltered from all external influence do not owe their development to the physical sunlight, so also education from without should not intervene before the cutting of the second teeth in the training of the memory. Very much to the contrary, the spontaneous growth of the memory will be noticeable, provided there is food for it within reach, and no attempt be made to train it by means of exterior methods.

This observation applies equally to the qualities belonging to the astral body before puberty. Provision should be made for their training, but bearing in mind that this body is still encompassed by a protecting shell. It is something wholly different to take care of the germs which are in process of development within the astral body before puberty and to expose the freed astral body after puberty to what it can assimilate in the outer world, without the protecting shell. This distinction is certainly very subtle, but without its careful consideration the whole significance of education cannot be understood.
chapters.p:
Songs and rhythm in the early years

In the early years it is especially important that things like children's songs make as beautiful a rhythmic impression on the senses as possible. What matters is the beautiful sound more than the meaning. The more something enlivens the eye and ear, the better. Do not underestimate the power to build up the organs that lies in dancing movements set to a musical rhythm.

About seven to puberty: pictures, example and guided imagination

With the change of teeth the life body throws off its outer covering. From then on it can be educated from outside. You need to be clear about what can work on the life body. Its change and growth mean the change and development of a person's leanings, habits, conscience, character, memory and temperament. You can work on the life body through pictures, through example, and by guiding the imagination in an orderly way. Up to seven the child needs a physical model it can imitate. In the same way, between the second teeth and puberty, the child's surroundings should hold everything that has an inner meaning and value toward which the child can turn its attention. Everything that works through picture and parable now has its rightful place.

The life body develops its strength when an orderly imagination can turn to living pictures and parables, whether seen or presented to the mind, and take guidance from them. What rightly works on the growing life body is the concrete, not the abstract, and concrete in a way that speaks to the mind and not only to the eye. Giving the child something to look up to inwardly is the right means of education in these years. So it is of the highest importance that the young person has, in the adults who bring them up, people whose own way of seeing things can awaken the right powers of mind and character in them.

Reverence and authority

Imitation and example are the key words for the early years. For the years we are now discussing the key words are reverence for a person and authority. [Note: this translation says "hero-worship".] Authority that comes naturally and is not forced must provide the inner standard by which the young person forms conscience, habits and leanings, brings their temperament into order and gains their own outlook on the world. The poet's fine words apply especially to this age: everyone must choose the hero whose path they will follow toward the heights.

Veneration and reverence are forces that help the life body grow in the right way. Anyone who was not able, in this period, to look up to someone with unlimited reverence will suffer for it for the rest of their life. Where this veneration is missing, the living forces of the life body wither. Picture the effect of the following on a child. An eight-year-old boy is told about a person who is held in very high regard. Everything he hears fills him with awe. The day comes when he is to see this person for the first time. A deep reverence comes over him when he hears the bell ring at the door behind which the person will appear. The beautiful feelings such an experience brings are among the lasting gains of a life. And a person is fortunate who can look up to their teachers as natural authorities all the time, and not only in life's high moments.

To these living authorities, people who embody moral and intellectual strength, must be added authorities met in the mind. The great examples of history and the stories of exemplary men and women should shape the conscience and the direction of the mind. Abstract moral principles should not. Those can only do their proper work once the astral body is freed from its covering at puberty.

Stories

History teaching especially should be guided by this. Before the second teeth, the stories and fairy tales told to a child can only aim at joy, refreshment and pleasure.

After that, you need to think ahead about what you tell, so that pictures of life which the young person can usefully try to live up to are set before their mind. Do not overlook the fact that bad habits can be driven out by pictures that are correspondingly off-putting. Warning against bad habits and tendencies does little good at best. But if you let the living picture of a person with that fault work on the young imagination, and show where the tendency leads, you do a great deal toward rooting it out.

Always keep in mind that the growing life body is affected by living pictures seen clearly in the mind, not by abstract ideas. Of course these pictures have to be used with the greatest tact, or the result will be the opposite of what you want. With stories, everything depends on how they are told. So telling a story aloud cannot be successfully replaced by reading it.

Teaching through images before concepts

Between the second teeth and puberty, the picture or symbol matters in another way too. The young person should come to know the secrets of nature and the laws of life as far as possible through symbols, not through dry intellectual ideas. Likenesses that show how things are inwardly connected should reach the child in such a way that the order and law behind them is sensed and guessed at more than grasped in concepts. The saying "everything that passes is only a likeness" should be a guiding motto for education in this period. It matters a great deal that a person receives the secrets of nature in likenesses before they meet them as natural laws. An example will make this clear. Suppose you want to speak to a young person about the immortality of the soul, about its leaving the body. You might compare it to the butterfly coming out of the chrysalis. As the butterfly comes out of the chrysalis, so the soul comes out of the shell of the body after death. No one will properly grasp the facts in abstract ideas who has not first received them through an image like this. Such a comparison speaks to feeling and to the whole inner life, and not to the intellect alone. A young person who has been through this comes to the subject in a quite different frame of mind when it is given to them later in intellectual terms. Indeed a person who cannot first approach the riddle of existence with this kind of feeling is much to be pitied. The teacher needs to have comparisons at hand for all the laws of nature and secrets of the world.

The teacher has to believe the image

Here it is clear how much spiritual science can enrich practical life. Someone who makes up comparisons out of a materialist, intellectual way of thinking and then presents them to young people will usually make little impression. Such a person has had to puzzle the comparisons out with their head. Comparisons you have not first made real for yourself do not convince the people you give them to. When you speak to someone in parables, they are affected by more than what you say or show. A fine inner current passes from speaker to hearer. Unless the speaker has a warm feeling of belief in the comparison, it will make no impression. To have the right effect you must believe in your comparisons as realities. That is only possible when you have the spiritual outlook and when the comparisons themselves come out of spiritual science. A real spiritual researcher does not have to strain over the comparison of the soul leaving the body, because for them it is a truth. For them the butterfly coming out of the chrysalis is the same event, at a lower level of nature, as the soul leaving the body at a higher level. They believe it with all their strength, and this belief flows as if in invisible streams from speaker to listener and carries conviction. Direct streams of life then flow from teacher to pupil. But for that the teacher has to draw from the full source of spiritual science. Their words, and everything that comes from them, need to be filled with feeling, warmth and glow from a true spiritual view of life. This opens a magnificent prospect for the whole of education. Once education lets itself be fed from the living source of spiritual science, it will be filled with deep vitality. It will stop the groping in the dark that is so common in this field. All teaching methods and all educational theories that do not keep drawing fresh sap from such roots are dried up and dead. Spiritual science has fitting comparisons for all the secrets of the world. They are not invented by the human mind. They are drawn from the nature of things and were laid down as a foundation by the forces of the world at creation. So spiritual science must be the basis for any approach to education.

Memory

One power that needs particular attention at this stage is memory. Developing the memory is bound up with the transformation of the life body. Since the life body becomes free between the second teeth and puberty, this is also the time when the memory should be looked after from outside. If what the memory needs is neglected in this period, it will be permanently less valuable to the person than it could have been. What is neglected here cannot be made up later.

An intellectual, materialist way of thinking easily leads to mistakes here. An approach to education that comes from it is easily prejudiced against whatever is learned by memory alone. It never tires of campaigning against mere memory training and uses the most ingenious methods to make sure the young person does not mechanically take in what they do not really understand. A purely intellectual, materialist view is easily convinced that the only way into things is through abstract ideas. Thinkers of this kind find it hard to accept that the other powers of the inner life are at least as necessary for understanding things as the intellect is. It is not just a figure of speech to say that we can understand with feeling and with the heart as well as with the intellect. Ideas are only one of the means of understanding the things of this world, and only to materialists do they seem the only means. Of course many people do not think of themselves as materialists and still consider intellectual understanding the only kind. They may claim an idealist or even a spiritual view of the world and of life. But the stance of their minds toward both is materialist. For the intellect is in fact the mind's instrument for grasping material things.

On the deeper foundations of understanding, let me quote from Jean Paul's excellent book on education, already mentioned. It is full of golden ideas about education and deserves far more attention than it gets. It is worth more to those bringing up children than many of the most highly regarded writings in this field. The passage runs:

[Steiner quotes Jean Paul:] "Do not be afraid of not being understood, even for whole sentences. Your look and your way of speaking, together with the child's eager wish to understand, make half of it clear, and with that half, and in time, the other half too. With children, the way a thing is said is half the language. Remember that they understand their language before they can speak it, as we understand Greek or any other foreign language before we can speak it. Trust time and context to do the deciphering. A five-year-old understands the words 'yet', 'truly', 'on the contrary', 'of course'. But for a definition of them you would have to ask the father, not the child! The little word 'but' reveals a small philosopher. If an eight-year-old with their growing speech is understood by a three-year-old, why should you narrow your language to the little one's babbling? Always speak several years ahead. With a one-year-old speak as if they were two, with a two-year-old as if they were six. In general, too much of learning is credited to the teacher. The teacher should remember that the child already has half its world, the inner half, such as its moral and deeper ideas, complete within itself. A language made only of concrete images can never give a child those ideas. It can only light them up. We can learn language from children as well as teach them by language, through bold and yet accurate word-painting, such as I have heard from three- and four-year-olds: 'leg-fish' for otter, 'air-mouse' for bat, and so on."

Learn first, understand later

This passage is about a different kind of understanding before intellectual grasp than the one we are discussing, but Jean Paul's words matter here too. The child takes the structure of language into its inner life without consciously using the laws of grammar. In the same way, for the sake of the memory, the young person should learn things they will only really understand later. What is first taken in during this period purely by memory is best turned into concepts afterward, just as you learn the rules of a language more easily once you can already speak it. All the talk about "learning by rote without understanding" is nothing more than a materialist prejudice. For instance, a child needs only a few examples to get the most necessary rules of multiplication, for which the fingers are far better suited than an abacus, and should then learn the times tables thoroughly by heart. If you go about it this way, you are taking the nature of the growing child into account. You can go wrong here if too much is asked of the intellect while the memory is forming. The intellect is a power of the mind that is only born at puberty, and it should not be worked on from outside before then. Until puberty the young person should take into memory the treasures humanity has thought through. Later is the time to work through with ideas what has been impressed on the memory. So a person should not only remember what they have understood. They should come to understand what they already know, that is, what they have already made their own through memory, as a child does in learning to speak. This applies widely. First take in historical events by memory, then grasp them through ideas. First impress geographical facts well on the memory, then understand how each thing relates to the rest. In certain respects all understanding through ideas should draw on what memory has stored. The more the young person already knows through memory before they come to understanding, the better. It hardly needs saying that all this applies only to the period we are speaking of and not to any later one. If you learn a subject later in life, the opposite order may be right and desirable, though even then much depends on the particular nature of the learner. But at the age we are discussing, the mind must not be dried out by being overloaded with intellectual ideas.

More than what the eye sees

It is also true that teaching purely from physical objects, if taken too far, comes from a materialist view of life. At this age every idea should point beyond itself. You should not be satisfied, for instance, with just showing the child a plant, a seed or a flower. Everything should be seen as a likeness of something spiritual. A seed is in truth more than what the eye sees. The whole new plant lives in it invisibly, and the child must really take in, with perception, imagination and feeling, that such a thing is more than the senses perceive. The mysterious presence of hidden life must really be felt. It cannot be objected that this would weaken plain observation. On the contrary, truth itself would lose out if we held only to what the senses perceive. The full reality of a thing exists in spirit and in matter, and observation can be just as careful when you bring the inner faculties to the study along with the physical senses. If people could see, as a spiritual researcher can, how both body and soul are harmed by mere object lessons, they would not lay so much stress on them. What is the use, from the highest point of view, of showing young people all kinds of physical experiments with minerals, plants and animals, if the study does not also awaken a feeling for the spiritual mystery behind what the senses show? A materialist mind will certainly make nothing of what has been said here, and the spiritual researcher knows that only too well. But it is just as clear to them that a truly practical way of educating can never come from a materialist mind. Such a mind thinks itself so practical and is in reality so impractical when it comes to dealing with life in a living way. Set against true reality, materialist opinions look like fantasies, while to the materialist the explanations of spiritual science must look just as fantastic. No doubt many obstacles remain to be overcome before the basic teachings of spiritual science, which arise from life itself, make their way into the art of education. That is to be expected, since these truths are still strange to many people. But if they really are the truth, they will become part of all culture.

Thinking, feeling and will

Only a firm conviction that these are the right means of working on young people lets the teacher find the right way to deal with each individual case. The teacher has to know how the separate powers of the inner life, thinking, feeling and will, should be treated, and how their development works back on the life body, which can be fully shaped by outside influences between the second teeth and puberty.

The foundations for a healthy, strong will can be laid by handling the first seven years in the way already described. Such a will needs the fully developed form of the physical body to support it. From the second teeth on, the task is to have the developing life body give the physical body the powers by which it can firm up its form. What makes the strongest impression on the life body also works most strongly to strengthen the physical body. And the strongest impulses are called up in the life body by perceptions and ideas through which a person feels and experiences their own relation to the eternal ground of the world, that is, by religious experiences. A person's will, and with it their character, will never develop healthily if they cannot have deep religious experiences at this age. A will formed as a unified whole makes a person feel they are a living part of the whole world. If a person does not feel firmly connected with a divine and spiritual reality, their will and character will remain unsteady, divided and unhealthy.

The life of feeling develops in the right direction through the likenesses and pictures already described, and especially through everything, from history or elsewhere, that shows people of character. Deep attention to the mysteries and beauties of nature is also important for building up the world of feeling. Here it is especially good to cultivate the sense of beauty and awaken a feeling for art. Music should give the life body the rhythm that then lets it sense the hidden rhythm in everything. A young person who does not receive the benefit of developing the musical sense in this period will miss a great deal in later life. For someone in whom this sense is wholly lacking, a certain side of the world must stay hidden. The other arts should by no means be neglected either. Awakening a sense for architectural form, for sculpted shape, for line and design, and for harmony of color: none of these should be left out of the plan of education. All of this can be done so simply, where circumstances require, that the objection "our circumstances do not allow it" can never hold. You can do a great deal with the simplest means if the teacher has the right sense for it. Joy in life, love of existence and strength for work all come to the whole person from cultivating the sense of beauty and art. And how much nobler and more beautiful the relations between people become through it! The moral sense, which in this period is being formed by pictures of life and by the people the child looks up to, also gains a certain firmness if, through the sense of beauty, the good is felt as beautiful and the bad as ugly.

Thinking in its own form, as an inner life of abstract ideas, must be kept in the background during this period. It should develop by itself, as it were, without being worked on from outside, while the mind is fed with likenesses and pictures of life and the secrets of nature. So thinking has to grow, and the power of judgment has to ripen, in the midst of the other inner experiences between seven and puberty. Then, after puberty, the person becomes able to form their own opinions about life and knowledge in complete independence. Indeed, the less you work directly on the critical faculty and the more you work indirectly, by developing the other powers, the better it will be for the person's whole later life.

Movement and games

Spiritual science gives principles for the purely physical side of education as well as the inner side. To take a typical example, consider gymnastics and children's games. Love and joy have to fill the surroundings in the first years. In the same way the growing life body must be led to really feel, through physical exercise, its own growth and ever-increasing strength. Gymnastic exercises, for instance, should be done in such a way that with every movement and every step the feeling rises in the boy or girl: "I feel strength growing in me." This feeling should show itself inwardly as healthy delight, as a sense of pleasure. To devise exercises of this kind, you need more than an intellectual knowledge of the anatomy and physiology of the human body. You need a close, intuitive, sympathetic knowledge of how joy and ease are connected with the postures and movements of the body. The person who designs such exercises should experience for themselves how one movement or posture brings a pleasant, easy feeling and another a loss of strength, and so on. The conviction that gymnastics and physical exercise can be developed in this direction can only come to the educator from spiritual science, or above all from a mind open to it. You do not even need the power of sight in the spiritual worlds, only the willingness to apply to life what spiritual science has given. If spiritual knowledge were applied in practical fields such as education, all the useless talk about how it still has to be proved would stop at once. For anyone who applied it rightly, this knowledge would prove itself throughout life by making them healthy and strong. They would see through and through that it is true in practice, and they would find that a better proof than any "logical" or so-called "scientific" argument. Spiritual truths are best known by their fruits. A supposed proof, however scientific, could hardly be more than logical sparring.

Puberty: independent judgment

At puberty the astral body is born. With the free outward development that follows, everything opened up by the world of outer perception, by one's own judgment and by free understanding first rushes in on the mind. It has already been said that these powers, not yet worked on directly, should be developed by the right use of educational means just as unconsciously as the eyes and ears develop in the womb. But with puberty the time has come when a person is ready to form their own judgment about what they have learned up to now. You can do a person no greater harm than to awaken their own judgment too early. A person should only judge when they have stored up what is needed for judging and comparing. If they form independent opinions before that, those opinions have no sure foundation. All one-sidedness in life, all the bleak "creeds" that rest on a few scraps of knowledge and presume to judge ideas that humanity has tested over long ages, go back to exactly this mistake in education. Before you are ready to think for yourself, you need to set before you what others have thought. There is no sound thinking that has not been preceded by a sound feeling for truth, supported by a natural authority. If you want to follow these principles of education, you must not let people think at too early an age that they are able to judge. By avoiding this you leave them free to let life work on them from every side, without prejudice. For a single judgment that does not rest on a rich store of inner treasure puts a stumbling block in the path of the person who makes it. Once you have pronounced a judgment on something, you are always influenced by having done so. You no longer take in an experience as you would have if you had not set up an opinion that is now tangled up with the matter. Young people should have the attitude of learning first and judging afterward. What the intellect has to say about a thing should only be said after all the other powers of the mind have spoken. Before that the intellect should only act as a go-between. It should only serve to take hold of what is seen and felt and to take it in as it is, without letting unripe judgment take over. So before this age the young person should be shielded from all theories about things, and the emphasis should be on meeting the experiences of life and taking them in. A growing person can certainly be told what people have thought about this or that. But you should avoid letting them form opinions that come from a judgment made too early. They should take in opinions with feeling, without deciding at once for one view or the other and without attaching themselves to a party, thinking as they listen: "One person said this, another said that." Above all, cultivating this attitude requires a great deal of tact from teachers and parents, and spiritual knowledge is exactly what can supply that tact.

Closing

It has only been possible to develop a few aspects of education in the light of spiritual science here. The intention was only to give a hint of the tasks of civilization this philosophy will have to take on. Whether it can do so depends on whether a feeling for this way of thinking spreads in wider and wider circles. For that to happen, two things are necessary. First, people need to give up their prejudice against spiritual science. Anyone who truly engages with it will soon see that it is not the fantastic nonsense so many people today imagine. This is not meant as a reproach to such people. Everything our time offers as education must at first produce the view that those who pursue spiritual science are dreamers. On the surface hardly any other view is possible, because there seems to be a complete contradiction between what is called spiritual science or Theosophy and everything present-day culture suggests as the basis of a healthy view of life. Only a deeper look shows how self-contradictory the views of the present must remain without these principles, how they in fact call for these very principles and cannot do without them in the long run. The second thing concerns the sound development of Theosophy itself. Life will only welcome Theosophy if those in Theosophical circles come to see everywhere that what matters is to make these teachings bear fruit as widely as possible in every area of life, and not just to theorize about them. Otherwise people will go on seeing Theosophy as a kind of religious sect fit only for a few fanatical enthusiasts. But if it does positive, useful work, the Theosophical movement cannot in the long run be refused an intelligent hearing.
